Take the L
TAYK thuh EL
verb phrase (Gen-Z slang)
From sports standings, where L marks a loss and W a win. "Take the L" (accept the loss) circulated in hip-hop and sports talk through the 2000s–2010s and became a Gen-Z and gaming staple; to "take an L" is to suffer a defeat or embarrassment, and to "take the L" is to admit it. Often shortened to just "L" as a verdict ("that’s an L").

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang to take the L is to accept a loss — a game, an argument, a rejection, an embarrassment — and move on, ideally without making excuses. "Just take the L, bro." As a habit it is surprisingly close to wisdom. The Christian observation: Scripture expects God’s people to lose, and to know how. "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16); "when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me" (Mic 7:8). Taking the L humbly is what Peter commands: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time" (1Pe 5:6). But the gospel turns the phrase inside out. Christ’s whole call is to take the L on purpose: "whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it" (Mat 16:25). Paul tallied his whole résumé and wrote it all in the loss column: "what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ" (Php 3:7). The cross looked like the greatest L in history and was the decisive W. A father tells his son: learn to lose a game without sulking and an argument without lying; and learn the bigger thing — that the man who will not lose anything for Christ loses everything, and the man who loses everything for Christ wins Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (sports and hip-hop; general 2010s) for accepting a loss without excuse — a humble habit Scripture commends, and a picture of the Christian life: losing for Christ to find life.

expand to see more

TAKE THE L, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang; from sports W–L records) To accept a loss, defeat, or embarrassment. "She said no. Just take the L."

Take an L, to suffer a loss; L alone as a verdict: "that’s an L," "massive L." Opposite: W, dub.

Gaming use: concede, move to the next match.

Webster (1828), root word loss: “LOSS, noun 1. privation, as the loss of property; loss of money by gaming; loss of health or reputation. every loss is not a detriment. we cannot regret the loss of bad company or of evil habits. 2. Destruction; ruin; as the loss of a ship at sea; the loss of an army. 3. Defeat; as the loss of a battle. 4. Waste; useless application;”

Decode for parents: a good phrase to borrow when teaching children to lose well.

Key Scripture

Pro 24:16 — "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief."

Mic 7:8 — "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me."

1Pe 5:6 — "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:"

Mat 16:25 — "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it."

Php 3:7 — "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ."

Modern Corruption

Take the L teaches a sound habit — admit defeat and move on; its only limit is that it treats loss as something to shrug off, where Scripture teaches losing for Christ as the way to life.

expand to see more

Little needs correcting here; the phrase is a small sermon against excuses. A boy who can say "I lost, my fault" is learning something many grown men never do. Proverbs builds the same muscle: the just man falls seven times and gets up again (Pro 24:16), and Peter commands humility under God’s hand (1Pe 5:6).

The gospel goes further than the slang. The world takes Ls reluctantly and hopes for Ws; Christ calls His followers to choose the loss: "whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it" (Mat 16:25). Paul put his pedigree, his learning, and his reputation in the loss column "for Christ" (Php 3:7). Teach your children to lose well at checkers so they can lose everything well for Him.
